Packaging ideas

Five ideas for a more memorable unboxing

FORME Packaging editorialUpdated October 21, 20263 min read

A considered opening uses a few clear gestures. Arrange the exterior, closure, interior and product information so the user understands what to do next.

In this guide1. Plan the opening sequence2. Give the contents a deliberate arrangement3. Coordinate texture and 4. Keep the message concise5. Make the next step usefulDiscuss your packaging →

1. Plan the opening sequence

Sketch what the recipient sees at each step: the outer shipping case, the presentation box, the message and the products. Remove repeated layers that do not protect anything or communicate a useful detail. A clear sequence can feel thoughtful without adding a complicated mechanism.

Keep the first opening gesture obvious. A ribbon pull should connect to the drawer; a front tuck tab should have room for fingers; a magnetic cover should open without forcing the base. Test the action with someone who has not seen the design brief.

2. Give the contents a deliberate arrangement

Position products in the order they are meant to be seen or used. Leave a consistent visual gap, but support each object so it cannot roll into the next. A shallow information card can sit above the tray if it does not crush the contents or prevent closure.

Check removal as carefully as presentation. A beautiful recess becomes frustrating if a bottle cannot be lifted out. Finger notches and pull ribbons should be designed into the support, rather than added after the insert is approved.

3. Coordinate texture and 4. Keep the message concise

Use texture where people naturally touch the pack: the lid edge, ribbon pull and outside paper. Choose a small set of coordinated surfaces. Review foil and embossing on the actual stock because their appearance changes with paper texture and lighting.

Place one clear welcome or product message where it will be read. If additional care instructions are needed, use a separate card or a readable panel. Decorative artwork should leave adequate space for information that the buyer actually needs.

5. Make the next step useful

After opening, customers may need storage guidance, refill instructions or a way to identify each item. Plan those details with the product team. Avoid relying on a dense block of tiny text hidden under an insert.

Prototype the complete pack and observe the whole sequence, including disposal or reuse of components. For subscriptions, test the printed mailer format; for a launch kit, compare a fitted rigid presentation. The right choice is the one that supports both handling and the brand experience.
